title: The marks of a great man
word: The marks of a great man
hook: the thirty-two marks and the good deeds said to cause them, read as poetry

segments.voice: Yesterday: a teaching that outlives its teacher, and your line, well proclaimed. Did you pass something on clearly? Today, an old list that's easy to misread, about a body. Day five hundred sixty-four.

Look closely at an old statue of the Buddha. There's a small round mark between the eyebrows. A rounded swelling on the crown of the head. Long earlobes. Sometimes a wheel carved on the sole of each foot. These aren't decorations a sculptor made up. They come from an old Indian list of thirty-two marks of a great man, signs that a person will become either a world ruler or a Buddha. The thirtieth Long Discourse, the Lakkhana Sutta, takes that list and asks a different question. Not what the marks are. Where they come from. Today: the marks of a great man.
screen: `A MARK BETWEEN THE EYEBROWS.` → `THIRTY-TWO MARKS.` → `WHERE DO THEY COME FROM?`

segments.voice: The Lakkhana Sutta goes through the marks in groups, and for each it tells what the Buddha did in earlier lives to earn it. Then it repeats the whole thing in verse. Here are a few. The wheels on the soles of his feet: because in past lives he brought happiness to many, took away fear and danger, and gave protection. Soft, tender hands, and fingers said to be webbed or net-like: because he drew people together in four ways, by giving, by kind words, by helpful action, and by treating people as equals. Deep blue eyes and lashes like a calf's: because he looked at people kindly, straight and openly, not sideways, not with suspicion. And the soft white tuft of hair between the eyebrows, the mark you see on statues: because he refused to lie. Read it that way and the list stops being strange. It becomes a portrait. A body shaped, over many lives, by what it did. Feet that carried people out of danger. Hands that gave and gathered. Eyes that looked kindly. A face that told the truth. You don't have to take the marks literally, and Buddhists themselves have understood them in different ways, as physical signs, as symbols, or as both. But the sutta's point is clear either way: deeds leave marks. And there's a kind of marking anyone can see in an ordinary face. The lines of someone who has smiled a lot. The steady eyes of someone who doesn't lie to you.
screen: `WHEELS: BRINGING PEOPLE HAPPINESS.` · `SOFT HANDS: GIVING AND GATHERING.` · `KIND EYES: LOOKING STRAIGHT.` · `THE TUFT: TELLING THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `THE MARKS OF KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind a kind face you know. Someone whose kindness shows. Look at it in your mind's eye. Where does the kindness live? In the eyes, the mouth, the way they tilt their head? Stay with that face for a while. Then, gently, feel your own face. Soften the eyes. Let the jaw loosen. Breathe. The bell holds the time.
The marks of a great man. In DN 30 each of the thirty-two marks is traced to a good deed: kind eyes from looking kindly, the tuft from telling the truth. Today's word.
screen: `THE MARKS OF A GREAT MAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the marks of kindness. Today, notice one kind face, and let yours look at people the way the sutta says: straight, open and kind. Day five hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Buddhist sculptors across Asia have followed the thirty-two marks for many centuries, most visibly the urna between the brows and the ushnisha on the crown, and teachers often explain each mark through the deed the Lakkhana Sutta links to it.

original.note: Pali lakkhana: mark, sign, characteristic. the thirty-two mahapurisa-lakkhana, marks of a great man.

trapdoor: what you thought: the marks on Buddha statues are just artistic style.
what it means: they come from a list of thirty-two marks, and DN 30 ties each to a deed of kindness.

what a scholar hears: the mahapurisa-lakkhana list is older than Buddhism's art; DN 30 pairs each mark with past-life conduct in prose and then verse, and the four sangaha-vatthu appear as the cause of the hand marks.

notes: DN 30 paraphrased. Please check each mark-to-deed pairing used: wheels on the soles (bringing happiness, removing fear, protection); soft hands and net-like (jala) hands (the four sangaha-vatthu); deep blue eyes and cow-like lashes (looking kindly, not askance); the urna (abstaining from false speech).
'Long earlobes' in the hook is from common iconography rather than the 32-mark list; confirm or remove.
'The list is older than Buddhism's art' / 'an old Indian list': confirm phrasing (the suttas present it as brahmanical lore).
